title: The Future of the Legal Profession: A Shared Vision — Opening Address at the Legal Profession Symposium 2025
pub: Supreme Court of Singapore / Singapore Judiciary (also published at (2026) 38 Singapore Academy of Law Journal)
author: Sundaresh Menon

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source does not engage the cluster’s central buyer-led workflow-unbundling and AI-pricing proposition. It instead reframes law-firm change around short-term profit incentives, superstar compensation and billable-hour-driven attrition among junior lawyers. This is relevant to the cluster’s staffing and billable-hour themes, but advances a materially different diagnosis rather than supporting or opposing the overall synthesis.
qs: These are just two aspects of modern legal practice that underscore its increasing focus on short-term profits and the bottom line, a trend that is likely to intensify.

st.an: The source reports task-specific legal-AI performance and predicts broad transformation of legal services, but it does not address access to justice, direct-to-consumer use, users’ verification capacity, remedies, or the downward transfer of risk. Its evidence therefore overlaps with the cluster’s augmentation discussion but is insufficient to establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.

These results inform us that generative AI will transform the legal services sector.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source reports strong performance on specified legal-work tasks and predicts broader transformation of legal services, but it does not address autonomous adjudication, consent, challenge rights, legal authority or legitimacy. Its evidence therefore supports capability claims without establishing a position on the cluster’s central proposition about machine judging.
qs: We see this in the landmark benchmark study that was published earlier this year by Vals AI, a US-based company that evaluates AI tools.(55) Through a series of real-world tasks, the study compared the performance of four legal AI tools against actual lawyers.

*All four tools *outperformed the lawyers in the summarisation of documents and the analysis of transcripts, and Harvey Assistant, the platform developed by the eponymous legal technology start-up, even outperformed the lawyers in three additional areas – data extraction, the generation of chronologies, and document review and analysis.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Menon accepts selective, human-led AI deployment: generative AI can improve routine work, but foundational expertise remains necessary to evaluate outputs. He materially extends the cluster by linking automation to the loss of junior apprenticeship tasks and proposing structured, intentional training and AI-enabled simulations to preserve professional development.
qs: 56) Some have also suggested that generative AI will fundamentally disrupt the traditional billable hour model, resulting in alternative fee structures becoming more common.(57) But leaving aside these predictions, what is certain is that generative AI can help our younger colleagues execute certain routine tasks more *efficiently *and at higher *quality*, and it can therefore make legal work more sustainable.

In particular, we must adopt a more structured and intentional approach to how we train them, which is precisely why the SAL has recently launched the Junior Lawyers Professional Certification Programme.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source directly endorses the cluster’s central proposition: AI may reduce the repetitive junior work through which foundational competence develops, even though that competence remains necessary to verify AI output. It likewise supports replacing incidental apprenticeship with more structured, intentional training, including possible AI-assisted methods.
qs: We have to think about this because traditionally, it was through the repeated performance of basic legal tasks, such as document review and drafting, that juniors developed their technical competencies and their basic lawyering skills.(59) But these learning opportunities will become more scarce given that these are precisely the same areas that generative AI tools excel in.

Nonetheless, it is essential that our young lawyers continue to develop these competencies and skills, because it would otherwise be impossible for them to meaningfully evaluate the output produced by these tools.

kp.k: Private practice faces structural sustainability pressures
kp.d: Menon frames sustainable private-practice careers as essential to the rule of law, public trust, renewal of the Bar and recruitment to the judiciary. He argues that expanding career alternatives, commercialisation, increasingly demanding work and diminished opportunities to develop professional skills combine into long-term structural challenges rather than problems admitting quick solutions.
qs: they are complex, long-term and structural in nature, and therefore unlikely to admit of quick or easy solutions.

kp.k: Expanding career alternatives intensify competition for young lawyers
kp.d: The address reports approximately 4,900 in-house counsel in Singapore, compared with around 2,800 in 2015, citing SAL statistics. International firms, overseas qualification routes and non-legal employers also expand alternatives. Menon welcomes these opportunities but warns that they can reduce the talent available to practise Singapore law; he explicitly treats movement in-house as circulation within the legal sector, not inherently a problem.
qs: we now have approximately 4,900 in-house counsels in Singapore.
we should see such movement as a circulation of talent

kp.k: Commercial pressures can undermine mentorship and professional purpose
kp.d: Menon argues that excessive emphasis on profitability and billable hours can crowd out training, ethical guidance and transmission of professional values. Reporting US developments rather than presenting them as equally prevalent in Singapore, he cites superstar compensation exceeding USD25 million and performance-based departures: three for every formal layoff, formal performance improvement plans more than doubling since 2021, and nearly 70 per cent of lawyers placed on such plans leaving within six months.
qs: the two specific developments that I have outlined are not as prevalent in Singapore as they are in the US
nearly 70 per cent of lawyers who are placed on such plans will leave their firms within six months.

kp.k: Complex litigation reduces opportunities for junior advocates
kp.d: The address links larger, more complex disputes and higher fees to clients preferring senior advocates, leaving juniors fewer opportunities for practical judgment and advocacy. As indicators, it reports £6.1 billion in 2024 revenue for the UK's fifty largest litigation practices, a 48 per cent increase over five years, and London Commercial Court median time to judgment increasing from 450 days in 2020 to 786 days in 2024. Menon announces forthcoming Practice Direction changes expecting junior oral submissions in specified appellate hearings and encouraging wider junior advocacy elsewhere.
qs: clients who pay significant legal fees will generally prefer senior lawyers to have conduct of their briefs.
Indeed, there is no substitute for being on one’s feet and making important judgment calls while engaging directly with the Bench, fellow counsel and witnesses.

kp.k: Surveyed entrants report substantial intentions to leave practice
kp.d: Surveys of applicants at the 2025 Mass Admission Ceremony and 2024 Mass Call found around 60% of respondents likely to move out of legal practice within five years and slightly more than a third likely to leave the legal profession entirely. The source's definition of legal practice includes the Judicial Service, Legal Service and Public Defender’s Office. Among those considering leaving their present jobs, excessive workload or poor work-life balance was cited by 79.9% in 2025 and 81.2% in 2024. Menon interprets the responses as primarily push factors; these are stated intentions, not measured subsequent departures.
qs: around 60% of the respondents indicated that they were likely to move out of legal practice within the next five years,
What this suggests is that our young lawyers are inclined to leave practice principally because of push factors

kp.k: Workforce data suggest earlier movement away from private practice
kp.d: Citing SAL statistics, Menon reports that in-house counsel account for around a quarter to a third of each cohort at the 2PQE, 3PQE and 4PQE marks, while private practice's share of the lawyer population declined from around 57% to 50% between 2015 and 2025 despite overall population growth. He also cites Adrian Tan's report that 310 lawyers with less than five years' PQE left the profession in 2021. These trends concern him insofar as they reflect reduced sustainability and attractiveness of private practice.
qs: while our total population of lawyers increased from 2015 to 2025, the proportion of lawyers in private practice declined over that same period from around 57% to 50%.
these trends are not *inherently *problematic.

kp.k: Unsustainable work threatens wellbeing, ethics and institutional renewal
kp.d: Menon identifies risks to talent retention, access to justice, renewal of the Bar and the quality and diversity of the Bench. He cites a Singapore survey in which three in ten lawyers screened positive for depression and four in ten for anxiety, and discusses ethical fading under pressure. As cross-sector supporting evidence, he reports McKinsey's analysis of 1,800 large companies associating stronger long-term performance and resilience with prioritising organisational capital; this is not presented as a law-firm-specific study.
qs: A recent survey found that three in ten lawyers in Singapore screened positive for depression, and four in ten for anxiety.
high pressure work environments contribute to employees making judgments that are not in keeping with high professional standards.

kp.k: Sustainability requires cultural change and concrete workplace practices
kp.d: Menon recommends craftsmanship, a shared mission of administering justice, openness, respect, mutual trust and expanded leadership training. He announces draft SAL Sustainability Principles for discussion and possible adoption, covering efficient meetings, mental-wellness resources, protected training and mentoring time, and clearer delegation with realistic, negotiable deadlines. Existing initiatives include Temasek's Lawyer Sustainability Guidelines, adopted internally and by ten key law-firm partners for Temasek matters.
qs: the implementation of policies to promote sustainable practices will be less effective if we do not work on these fundamental steps.
This calls on firms to provide resources to promote mental wellness, and to set aside protected time for training and mentoring.

kp.k: Agentic AI extends capabilities into multi-step task execution
kp.d: Referring to OpenAI's 17 July 2025 announcement, Menon describes ChatGPT agent as combining website interaction, information synthesis and conversational intelligence. He reports claimed capabilities to navigate websites, filter results, request secure user login, run code, analyse information and produce editable slideshows and spreadsheets. These are attributed descriptions of a newly launched system, not results of legal-work testing.
qs: ChatGPT agent is said to be able to complete online tasks on behalf of the user through a process that involves *reasoning *and *action*.

kp.k: Vals AI benchmark indicates advantages on specific legal tasks
kp.d: Menon reports that a Vals AI study published earlier in 2025 compared four legal AI tools with actual lawyers on real-world tasks. According to his account, all four outperformed lawyers in document summarisation and transcript analysis; Harvey Assistant additionally outperformed them in data extraction, chronology generation, and document review and analysis. The address supplies no scores or participant sample size and presents these task-level findings as evidence of potential to reshape legal delivery.
qs: Through a series of real-world tasks, the study compared the performance of four legal AI tools against actual lawyers.

Harvey Assistant, the platform developed by the eponymous legal technology start-up, even outperformed the lawyers in three additional areas – data extraction, the generation of chronologies, and document review and analysis.

kp.k: AI efficiency supports sustainability; pricing disruption remains predictive
kp.d: Menon endorses AI's capacity to improve efficiency and quality in certain routine junior tasks and recommends widespread, informed and effective use. He separately reports John Quinn's suggestion that failing to use AI in trial preparation may soon constitute malpractice in the US, and others' predictions that AI will disrupt hourly billing and increase alternative fees. He explicitly sets those predictions aside when advancing the sustainability case. SAL and Microsoft have developed a foundational generative-AI and prompt-engineering course, supplemented by SAL guidance and an instructional video.
qs: Some have also suggested that generative AI will fundamentally disrupt the traditional billable hour model, resulting in alternative fee structures becoming more common.
Hence, we should encourage equipping the profession with the skills to enable the widespread, informed and effective use of generative AI.

kp.k: Automation threatens the traditional apprenticeship learning pathway
kp.d: Menon predicts that AI proficiency in document review and drafting will make repeated basic-task learning opportunities scarcer. He argues that juniors must nevertheless acquire technical competencies and basic lawyering skills to meaningfully evaluate AI-generated output. His recommended response is structured, intentional training rather than assuming traditional work allocation will continue to develop those capabilities.
qs: traditionally, it was through the repeated performance of basic legal tasks, such as document review and drafting, that juniors developed their technical competencies and their basic lawyering skills.

Nonetheless, it is essential that our young lawyers continue to develop these competencies and skills, because it would otherwise be impossible for them to meaningfully evaluate the output produced by these tools.

kp.k: Structured programmes and AI simulations offer training alternatives
kp.d: Menon connects the recently launched SAL Junior Lawyers Professional Certification Programme to the need for more deliberate training. He also proposes AI itself as a training tool, citing Three Crowns and Stanford CodeX's February 2025 announcement of an AI-powered cross-examination platform offering tailored scenarios, actionable feedback and customisation. This is an example of an announced training approach, not evidence of measured learning outcomes.
qs: We must therefore reimagine the way in which we train our young lawyers.
will allow users to practice in realistic scenarios tailored to different fact patterns, receive detailed and actionable feedback, and customise their training

kp.k: Human judgment and relationships gain importance alongside AI
kp.d: Menon predicts increased emphasis on critical thinking, persuasion, integrating technology into legal work and building trusted client relationships. He argues that these capabilities require sustained mentorship and that involving juniors in higher-order work can strengthen professional purpose and support sustainable careers.
qs: generative AI will also reshape the expectations of what is needed for successful lawyering.
The growing emphasis on these core qualities will increase the need for proper and sustained mentorship, since these qualities are invariably better caught rather than they are taught.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Menon argues that generative AI will transform legal services, can improve routine work and career sustainability, and will require changes to junior training and the skills valued in lawyers.
pts.d: In paragraphs 51–56, Menon claims that AI can help junior lawyers perform certain routine tasks more efficiently and at higher quality, making practice more sustainable. He also predicts that AI will reduce opportunities to acquire foundational competencies through repeated document review and drafting, requiring more structured and intentional training. Those competencies remain necessary to check AI output meaningfully. AI itself might support training, including simulated cross-examination. Menon further predicts a premium on critical thinking, persuasion, technology integration and trusted client relationships, increasing the need for sustained mentorship. He reports, but explicitly sets aside, predictions about malpractice for not using AI in trial preparation and disruption of hourly billing; these are not presented as his own firm conclusions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal empirical basis is Menon's account of Vals AI's 2025 comparison of legal AI tools with lawyers; training and mentorship claims rely on professional reasoning and an announced training platform.
pts.d: Menon cites Vals AI, an independent evaluator rather than Harvey's own benchmarking effort, as comparing four legal AI tools against lawyers on real-world tasks. He reports that all four exceeded lawyer performance on document summarisation and transcript analysis, with Harvey Assistant also exceeding lawyer performance on data extraction, chronology generation, and document review and analysis. The address does not supply numerical scores, sample sizes or methodological details. His prediction of fewer learning opportunities rests on the overlap between tasks AI performs well and traditional junior training tasks. The Three Crowns–Codex cross-examination platform announcement of 12 February 2025 illustrates potential AI-assisted training, rather than demonstrated training outcomes. SAL's foundational AI course, guidance and Junior Lawyers Professional Certification Programme are institutional responses, not evidence of measured effects on retention or sustainability. No separate empirical study is offered for the predicted premium on human skills and mentorship.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The address describes present capabilities as of July 2025 and anticipates further professional changes without specifying a deadline; informed adoption and preserved legal competence are central qualifications.
pts.d: The temporal anchor is the address delivered on 29 July 2025. Menon describes the Vals AI study as published earlier that year and refers to ChatGPT agent's launch less than two weeks earlier. Routine-task benefits are framed as already available, while transformation of training and professional expectations is prospective with no quantified adoption horizon. His productivity claim concerns certain routine tasks, not all legal work or autonomous replacement of lawyers. He calls for skills supporting widespread, informed and effective use and insists juniors retain the ability to assess AI output. AI-assisted training is expressed as a possibility. The reported malpractice prediction uses 'soon' and is qualified geographically to at least the US; it and the alternative-fee prediction are explicitly set aside rather than adopted as certainties.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Junior lawyers in Singapore private practice are the central affected group, alongside senior mentors, law firms, professional training bodies and clients.
pts.d: Junior lawyers could gain relief from routine tasks but lose some traditional learning-by-doing opportunities. Senior lawyers would face greater responsibility for sustained mentorship in higher-order skills and client relationships. Law firms and professional bodies would need to support informed AI adoption and redesign training. Clients feature chiefly through the continued importance of trust and meaningful relationships, rather than a quantified prediction of lower fees or improved access to justice. The framing is principally augmentation with human checking of AI output, not wholesale replacement of lawyers. Menon does not forecast AI-driven headcount reductions, staffing ratios or displacement into in-house roles; the earlier attrition statistics concern the broader sustainability context and are not attributed to AI.
